title: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech
gist: The Consumer Technology Association estimates that fully reshoring 10 consumer electronics categories to the US by 2031 would cost $185-230B in capex, 555-668k workers and raise prices 27-55% on average, with smartphones hit hardest (+152%). It proposes an assembly-only first step costing $16-19B instead.

insights.claim: The CTA estimates that fully US-made production of 10 common consumer electronics categories by 2031 would require $185-230 billion of capital expenditure, 555,000-668,000 additional full-time employees and 19.1-19.5 billion kWh of electricity per year.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sizes the capex and labor bill behind US tech reshoring; implies slow, expensive execution rather than a quick supply-chain shift.
insights.quote: would require between $185 and $230 billion in capital expenditure, 555,000 to 668,000 additional full-time employees

insights.claim: The labor demand of full reshoring, more than double the existing US computer and electronics manufacturing workforce, may be a bigger obstacle than the capital cost.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
entities: US computer and electronics manufacturing workforce
insights.so_what: Labor availability is a binding constraint on reshoring timelines; watch US manufacturing hiring and wage data.

insights.claim: Reshoring all supply chains at once would compete for electricity with AI data center demand over the same period.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Reshoring and AI buildout both draw on a constrained power grid, a link to power and utilities names.

insights.claim: Taking current tariffs into account, fully manufacturing a smartphone in the US would raise its cost by 152 percent, the highest among the 10 categories, versus 93 percent for laptops, 97 percent for smartwatches and 41 percent for TVs.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Products with processors, memory and advanced displays are the most exposed; hardware makers with high smartphone/laptop mix face the largest margin or price pressure.
insights.locator: Smartphones are in a league of their own

insights.claim: The CTA expects companies to pass on only 25-50 percent of reshoring cost increases, producing a weighted average consumer price increase of 27-55 percent across the 10 categories, with the rest absorbed in margins.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Cost absorption implies margin compression for device makers if reshoring is forced.
insights.quote: the 10 products in our report would see a weighted average price increase of 27 to 55 percent

insights.claim: Higher device prices hit households already delaying tech purchases amid rising rent, grocery and fuel costs, and fewer units sold over time would worsen margins and could spook investors, making reshoring harder to finance.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A demand-elasticity loop (higher prices, fewer sales, lower margins, less investment) undermines the reshoring premise.

insights.claim: The CTA warns that modeled reshoring costs are highest in the categories consumers consider most essential, led by smartphones and laptops.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Policy that treats all consumer tech as one reshoring target hits consumers hardest where economics are worst.
insights.quote: The categories consumers regard as most essential, led by smartphones and laptops, are exactly those where the modeled cost of full domestic production is highest.

insights.claim: The CTA recommends reshoring only assembly first, estimated at $16-19 billion, which would still raise smartphone manufacturing cost by 67 percent and laptops by 50 percent but let firms keep sourcing components from trusted partners.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A staged assembly-first path is the industry-preferred compromise; watch for policy movement toward it.
insights.locator: Trump unlikely to embrace CTA's alternative plan

insights.claim: The CTA argues tariffs on component parts raise US assembly costs relative to the current import mix and should be paused or removed for components from trusted allies.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Component tariff relief is the lever that would lower reshoring costs; tariff changes are a signal for device makers' margins.
insights.quote: Component tariffs drive up US assembly costs relative to the current import mix

insights.claim: CTA executive chair Gary Shapiro said Trump's demand to move over 50 percent of semiconductor manufacturing to the US by the end of his term, roughly two years away, is physically and labor-wise impossible.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Industry leadership openly disputes the semiconductor reshoring timeline; expect a gap between policy targets and delivery.

insights.claim: Wall Street analysts forecast last spring that a US-made iPhone could cost $1,500-$3,500, and a former Apple manufacturing engineer said hiring enough US workers to meet global iPhone demand would be impossible.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Full US iPhone production is not credible near term; Apple's India shift continues to draw tariff threats.
insights.locator: Apple won't blame Trump for price increases

insights.claim: Apple's new $2,000 starting tier for the foldable iPhone Duo and ~$2,000 2T iPhone 17 Pro Max tier have drawn suspicion that they reflect tariff or reshoring cost anticipation, though Apple denies a link.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Premium-tier pricing tests may signal margin defense; track Apple ASP and gross margin commentary.

insights.claim: The CTA notes that small businesses represent 80 percent of its membership and cannot absorb Trump-era cost shocks the way Big Tech can, and that higher costs could measurably affect US inflation, which is already above target and rising.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Reshoring cost pass-through adds to inflation pressure and hits smaller hardware firms more than mega-caps.
